english: What this means for your contest category

CQ WW rule VIII.2 counts “a CW decoder, DX cluster, DX spotting Web sites … local or remote call sign and frequency decoding technology (e.g., CW Skimmer or Reverse Beacon Network)” as QSO-finding assistance. Using any of them places the entry in Single Operator Assisted (V.A.2) instead of Single Operator (V.A.1).

english: ARRL contests call it spotting assistance and name “PSKReporter, Telnet, DX spotting websites or bulletin board systems, automated multi-channel decoders”. Single Operator may not use it (HCAT.1.1: “Use of spotting assistance is not permitted.”). Single Operator Unlimited may (HCAT.2.1). ARRL’s glossary defines a multi-channel decoder as software that “displays multiple decoded signals at the same time”. Nexus decodes one signal at a time, so that definition does not describe its CW decoder. It does describe the cluster, RBN and PSK Reporter feeds.

Some of that is normal: when the squelch opens partway through a burst the start of the packet is lost, and a part-heard packet can never pass. The burst is CLIPPING (peaked {{peak}}, {{samples}} sample(s) at the rails) — lower the rig's USB AF output level, or the Windows input level for that device. Packet survives a lot of clipping, so this costs headroom rather than decodes, but there is no reason to run into the rails.

Software FSK timing is casual/Field-Day grade; AFSK is the timing-cleanest path.
